guides.title: Repairing Broken GRUB Bootloader via Live USB (chroot)
guides.symptom: Linux boots into 'grub rescue>' prompt, black screen, or boots directly into BIOS
guides.description: Rescue a broken GRUB2 bootloader using a Live Linux USB environment and `chroot` to reinstall EFI boot records.
causes: Windows Update or BIOS reset wiping the NVRAM boot variable
Corrupted `/boot/grub/grub.cfg` file pointing to missing partition UUID
guides.whyItWorks: Using `chroot` (change root) allows you to enter your installed Linux system from a Live USB session. Inside the chroot, running `grub-install` writes fresh binaries to the EFI System Partition (ESP) and `update-grub` auto-detects all kernels and operating systems.

steps.instruction: Boot from any Live Linux USB (Ubuntu/Fedora/Debian)
steps.detail: Insert a bootable Live USB, enter your PC's boot selection menu (usually F12, F11, or Esc), and select 'Try Ubuntu' (or live session). Open Terminal.

steps.instruction: Identify your Linux root partition and EFI partition
steps.detail:
Run:
sudo lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,LABEL
Identify your main Linux root partition (e.g. `/dev/nvme0n1p2` or `/dev/sda2`, typically ext4/btrfs) and your EFI System Partition (usually ~100-512MB, vfat/FAT32, e.g. `/dev/nvme0n1p1`).

steps.instruction: Mount the system partitions and bind virtual filesystems
steps.detail:
Replace `sda2` with your root partition and `sda1` with your EFI partition:
sudo mount /dev/sda2 /mnt
sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/boot/efi
for i in /dev /dev/pts /proc /sys /run; do sudo mount -B $i /mnt$i; done

Run:
sudo chroot /mnt
grub-install /dev/sda
update-grub
Type `exit` to leave the chroot, then reboot without the USB. Your GRUB menu will reappear cleanly.
steps.warning: Ensure you specify the disk (e.g. /dev/sda or /dev/nvme0n1), not the partition number when running grub-install on legacy systems, or let EFI handler manage it.

guides.title: Fixing Black Screen After NVIDIA Driver Updates & Wayland Issues
guides.symptom: Linux boots into a black screen, flashing cursor, or low-resolution fallback mode after graphics update
guides.description: Recover from broken NVIDIA proprietary drivers, blacklist conflicting Nouveau open-source drivers, and switch between Wayland and X11.
causes: Kernel updated without building matching NVIDIA Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) headers
Nouveau open-source driver conflicting with proprietary NVIDIA driver
Wayland display server incompatibility with older NVIDIA drivers
guides.whyItWorks: When the display manager (GDM/SDDM) fails to start due to a graphics driver mismatch, Linux drops to a black screen. Switching to a text virtual console (TTY) allows you to purge broken drivers, install matched DKMS modules, or fall back to stable drivers.

steps.detail: At the black screen or flashing cursor, press Ctrl + Alt + F3 (or F4 / F5). A full-screen text login prompt will appear. Enter your Linux username and password.

Run this command to completely remove the broken driver packages:
sudo apt purge '*nvidia*' -y
sudo apt autoremove -y

Let the driver subsystem detect your card and install the certified stable driver:
sudo ubuntu-drivers autoinstall
Or manually specify the LTS driver (e.g., `sudo apt install nvidia-driver-535 -y`).

steps.instruction: Force X11 fallback if Wayland continues to freeze
steps.detail:
Edit GDM configuration:
sudo nano /etc/gdm3/custom.conf
Find the line `#WaylandEnable=false` and remove the `#` to uncomment it so it reads:
WaylandEnable=false
Press Ctrl+O to save and Ctrl+X to exit. Then reboot with `sudo reboot`.

guides.title: Repair Corrupted Filesystems in Emergency Mode (`fsck`)
guides.symptom: Linux boot drops into 'Emergency Mode' or 'initramfs' prompt: 'UNEXPECTED INCONSISTENCY; RUN fsck MANUALLY'
guides.description: Fix corrupted ext4 and btrfs file system superblocks, repair bad inodes, and resolve fstab UUID mounting conflicts.
causes: Unclean shutdown due to power outage or forced hard power-off
Damaged file system journal or corrupt superblock metadata
guides.whyItWorks: `fsck` (File System Consistency Check) inspects cylinder groups, verifies inode counts, clears orphaned inodes, and restores journal integrity. Running it with the `-y` flag answers yes to repairing discovered inconsistencies.

steps.instruction: Identify the corrupted partition from the error message
steps.detail:
Read the on-screen emergency mode prompt. It will state the exact device path with inconsistencies, for example:
`/dev/sda2: UNEXPECTED INCONSISTENCY; RUN fsck MANUALLY.`

At the `(initramfs)` or root emergency prompt, run:
fsck -y /dev/sda2
(Replace `/dev/sda2` with your actual partition name). Allow the utility to pass through all 5 phases (inodes, blocks, directory structures, reference counts).

Once fsck finishes reporting 'FILE SYSTEM WAS MODIFIED', type:
exit
Or:
reboot
Your Linux distribution will now boot normally into the graphical desktop.
